docs.title: SYNK — About us
paragraphs: SYNK builds a personalization engine. We started with Korean education. In classrooms in Ulaanbaatar, we saw that every student had different strengths, got stuck in different places, and had different reasons for learning, so we set out to use technology to teach each student in a way that fits them. The engine we built is Atlas.

SYNK LAB — Learn Korean and develop your own judgment. LAB prepares learners for studying in Korea and the life that follows. With TOPIK Level 4 as a clear goal, learners also gain experience using Korean in real situations. We want to help people use AI while being able to explain their own thinking and judge the results.

SYNK SHIFT — Start with one task. Put personalization to work. SHIFT starts with one task where customers or staff need different guidance. We define who should complete what, then connect company materials and specialist modules with the shared Atlas engines. After introduction, we refine the service with the responsible team by checking actual use and the work needed to operate it.

SYNK PULSE — Films for brands fit their purpose; our own work invites a second look. For a film a brand commissions, we first decide where it will be used and who will see it. PULSE’s own music, videos, and character stories aim to be work you want to hear and see again. Both use two of Atlas’s engines in production: Loom, which composes the screen, and Reed, which handles sound.

SYNK PATH — Bring your own choices to travel and life in a new place. A good day in the same city looks different to each traveler, just as each person has different goals for life in Korea. PATH helps shape plans around the experiences you want, your budget and where you are now. Preferences you confirm can inform your next trip, while learning and project experience can support your study and career plans.
Each brand’s website explains which experiences are available now and which services are still in preparation.

We also prepare study and career plans for Korea, Korean and VR practice, portfolios, and connections with schools and employers. Housing, settling-in support, visits and cultural experiences in Korea are being prepared with partner operators.

I wanted to care for each student properly. When I worked at an academy in Mongolia, I knew each student needed different help, but I never had the time to tailor it to every one of them. I started SYNK to do that work with technology.

On SHIFT, the founder shares the process of building a company with AI and the decisions made along the way. We publish the approaches tried, failures, and reasons for revisions so others can draw on them in their own work.

Architecture gave me an eye for structure, psychology an interest in how people think and act, and the stage the experience of making something together with others. Today I put all of this into planning and building SYNK.”

Atlas is the personalization engine SYNK builds, and the name for its eight engines together. They share the work, from deciding what a person needs to ordering what to learn, giving explanations and hints, shaping screens and sound, and checking whether the help worked. LAB, SHIFT, PULSE, and PATH each pick the engines they need and fit them to their own services.

The same person needs different practice as their goals change. The expressions you need when preparing to study in Korea, working with a Korean company, or talking with family are not the same. We are developing Atlas to adjust tasks and explanations to the goals you set and your recent results, not to your age.

Core — Judging what is needed now. It looks at what the person is trying to do and where they get stuck, and decides what to do next and what help is needed. It also sets out the reasons for what it recommends and leaves out.
Loom — Scenes that respond to your touch. Combines soft materials, light, and movement to create interfaces and characters, with scenes that respond naturally to the user's actions.

Vellum — Explanations that make sense. Offers explanations and hints suited to the current task and the person’s own answer. Explains why the practice matters and what to look at when the student gets stuck.
Trail — Tracking practice and progress. Records the tasks completed and the help received. Lets learners compare earlier and recent answers to see what has changed.
Prism — Comparing learning results. Finds recurring difficulties and differences across learning examples. Highlights which content and explanations need a closer look.
Temper — Checking whether support helped. Checks whether a person can now do it on their own after a hint or practice activity, then uses those results to improve tasks and support.
Reed — Music and sound for each scene. Handles music and sound for creative work and learning scenes. Decides when to use sound, for example turning it down when someone needs to focus.

Strata (in development) — A map of what to learn next. Connects grammar, expressions, and vocabulary by difficulty and prerequisites. Helps identify the learning needed for a goal and which basics to revisit after a mistake.
LAB — Adjusts Korean practice, games, and hints to each learner’s goals and the results of what they tried.
SHIFT — We prepare to introduce personalization for one task. Purchasing advice, usage guidance, coaching and staff training are candidate use cases.
PULSE — Uses Loom, which composes the screen, and Reed, which handles sound, to make ad and model videos and music and character content.
PATH — Adjusts practice for life in Korea and interviews to each learner's intended major, career plans, and Korean level.

docs.title: SYNK LAB — Learning
paragraphs: SYNK LAB is an edtech company developing Korean textbooks, learning games, and a learning app built on Atlas, our personalization engine. We are preparing a one-year, in-person program targeting TOPIK Level 4, along with conversation classes with native Korean teachers and global English classes. Our approach connects cultural experiences, AI use, and collaborative projects to prepare learners for studying and living in Korea.

Learn Korean and learn to think for yourself. LAB prepares learners for studying in Korea and for life beyond it. TOPIK Level 4 is a clear goal, supported by experience using Korean in real situations. Learners use AI while building the ability to explain their own thinking and judge the results.

We are preparing education for everyone who wants to learn Korean. We look at the Korean learners need in daily life, study, and work, and are developing the curriculum, textbooks, and student app as we prepare to open.
What students write and the answers they choose feed into the next task and feedback. The conditions and schedule for each course are announced separately, and learning results are not guaranteed.
Edtech for personalized Korean learning

LAB is preparing Korean education for anyone who wants to learn the language, with no limit by nationality or where you live. Lessons are planned around where you want to use Korean and how much you can do now.

We are developing the curriculum, textbooks, and student app while preparing to open. Who each online or in-person course is for, its starting level, and the conditions for joining are announced course by course.

We first explore what learners want to do in Korean and what they find difficult. We are preparing classes in which students use what they have learned in real situations, receive feedback, and practice again in the next task.

Practice includes asking questions in university classes, explaining what you enjoy, and sharing opinions in team activities. We are preparing different ways to participate, including planning and editing as well as speaking and writing.

The classroom scenes on this website are examples explaining our approach. They are not actual student records or verified learning outcomes. Each student’s learning outcomes must be assessed through actual classes and experience.
SYNK LAB’s textbooks comprise six Synapse Core grammar books and two Synapse Talk conversation books—eight in total. The manuscripts are complete, and we are preparing for publication.

The learning goals for each Synapse Core book are:
Book 1 · TOPIK Level 1 — Read Hangul and introduce yourself.
Book 2 · TOPIK Level 2 — Build basic sentence patterns for everyday conversation.
Book 3 · TOPIK Levels 2–3 — Talk naturally about familiar everyday situations.
Book 4 · TOPIK Level 3 — Share your opinion and explain your reasons.
Book 5 · TOPIK Levels 3–4 — Explain your views on social issues.
Book 6 · TOPIK Levels 4–5 — Discuss specialist and abstract topics.

Synapse Talk Book 1 covers beginner conversation and connects with Core Books 1–2. Book 2 covers intermediate conversation and connects with Core Books 3–5. The conversation books cover material through TOPIK Level 4.

The levels indicate each book’s learning goals, not a guarantee of passing. The manuscripts are complete, but final review and publication are still in preparation. Publication dates and access details will be announced separately.

SYNK LAB is preparing 10 minigames. On the LAB page you can watch real gameplay from eight Korean games: Korean Racing, Words in Rhythm, Wind Run, Order Rush and Talk Rally practise listening, while The Teacher Is Back, Entry Check and Blank Slice practise reading. All eight are prototypes.

Race along a coastal road with Marin or Kkamong, listen to a Korean question, and answer by driving into a picture or word lane. Correct answers trigger a boost. The prototype includes 2,000 basic and extended vocabulary items, 400 learning stages of five words, and 2,008 word and guidance voice clips. All stages share one coastal course; the vocabulary list does not guarantee coverage of every TOPIK Level 1–2 item. Use A/D or arrow keys, or mobile steering and answer buttons.

Narration sequences each question, word pronunciation, and correct/incorrect feedback. Engine volume falls while speech plays, and the car waits before the gate until the question finishes. Replay, optional listening captions, pronunciation after the race, and a review that prioritizes mistakes support practice. The commentary is scripted audio, rather than live AI conversation.

Listening connects word sounds with pictures and spelling; reading practises recognizing spelling and meaning. Words in Rhythm plays three of our own Korean songs across two lanes. Listen to a narrated sentence and question, then answer O/X. Music quietens and regular notes clear during narration. Practise understanding times, places, reasons, conditions and changed information, with timing and listening answers checked separately and new spoken review questions. Speaking and writing extend expressions into offline dialogue and sentence tasks. The games currently provide no pronunciation or free-writing assessment. TOPIK I tests listening and reading; TOPIK II includes writing, while TOPIK Speaking is a separate test.

In Wind Run you hear 16 short requests such as “Take the left path.” or “Jump over the low fence.” and act them out. While you run there is only sound, no text; the text appears in the practice before the run and the review after it. In Order Rush you hear café orders and make each drink, matching the number of cups, the temperature and what to leave out. In Talk Rally, Mongle says something in Korean as it hits the ball, and you hit it back toward the reply card that fits. In The Teacher Is Back you read the requests in a story and move Marin and Kkamong to tidy the classroom, then read new, changed requests at the end. In Entry Check you read a notice, check each guest’s ticket, bags and words, and stamp pass or reject. In Blank Slice you read a sentence with a blank and slash the one word piece out of four that fits.

A meta-analysis of digital game-based second-language learning reported a between-group effect size of d=0.50 (Dixon et al., 2022). A retrieval-practice meta-analysis covering 222 studies and 48,478 learners reported g=0.499 (Yang et al., 2021). Picture-and-audio effects vary with materials and pacing (Reinwein, 2012). These findings inform our recall, feedback, short-audio, and replay design. Effect sizes are not percentage improvements, and SYNK-specific TOPIK gains and long-term learning outcomes have not yet been tested with learners. Primary sources are linked in the learning showcase.

We are preparing a path from minigames and offline learning toward TOPIK Level 1, followed by everyday-life content and village NPC conversations. The planned unlock follows an in-app TOPIK Level 1+ foundation stage and does not require an official score report. The full ten-game set, classroom-to-village integration, and NPC connection are still in preparation. The games store anonymous progress in this browser only, racing’s automated demonstrations are left out of learning records, and nothing connects to student accounts or a server.
Use Korean learned from textbooks in games. LAB is developing an app that adjusts subsequent tasks and feedback using students’ answers and the areas where they needed help.
Practise Korean for real situations. In five listening games and three reading games, you act directly on the requests you hear and the notices you read. Understanding Korean leads to action.

We create games with clear roles and goals, based on grammar from Synapse Core and conversations from Synapse Talk. Scenes and characters help students understand the situation and take part themselves.

In Words in Rhythm, listen to a narrated sentence and question, then press one of two O/X buttons on the beat. Music quietens and regular notes clear during the voice. Rhythm timing and listening answers are checked separately, followed by explanations and new spoken review questions.
We are developing a way to record sentences written and answers chosen in games, so they can inform later practice and feedback.

Find a way of learning that suits you. We first ask why students are learning Korean and how they prefer to study. We consider their answers, revisions, and teacher observations together to understand their strengths and difficulties.
At the start, we ask about learning goals, the preferred order of explanations, when hints are needed, and how students want to receive feedback.
We distinguish what students tell us, actual learning records, and AI inferences. We do not judge personality or ability from a single choice or favorite character.
We are preparing settings that can change as goals or study preferences change. Students will be able to correct anything the app has misunderstood.

Tasks adapt to your learning record. We are developing an app that adjusts task topics, hints, and feedback to learners’ goals and records. Difficult expressions come back for practice, and we check whether students can use them without help.

We are preparing an app that adjusts the order of example sentences and grammar explanations, hints and feedback to each student. In the public rhythm game you choose the song and rhythm difficulty yourself, and you can see an explanation for each question and review with new sentences.

We record first drafts, revisions, and hint use separately. The design lets teachers review AI summaries alongside the student’s actual circumstances and arrange further practice of difficult expressions in a new task.
We are developing an app that brings together mascot guidance, today’s task, feedback, and learning records. Practice informs the next task and its feedback.
Preparing a Korean patent application. Application planned for 2028.

Before class, a dance-trained instructor guides K-POP rhythm and basic movements. During class, learners connect movement with Korean expressions. After-class co-creation is an optional program for students who want to join. They choose a role in planning, scripting, performing, or editing, and can take part without performing or being filmed.

Students discuss what to make, listen to one another, explain their reasons in Korean, and check and revise ideas suggested by AI. Creating something together gives them practice in critical thinking, discussion, collaboration, and responsible use of AI—skills they will need in an AI era.

Before class · K-POP warm-up with a professional instructor — An instructor who majored in dance demonstrates K-POP rhythms and basic movements and practices them with students. Activity intensity and duration are adjusted to students’ physical condition. Learners warm up to music they enjoy and catch their breath before joining Korean class.

During class · Connect movements with expressions — Connect words used in the activity, such as 돌다 (turn), 멈추다 (stop), and 함께 (together), with movements that express their meanings. In the fixed 30 minutes of group speaking within a 90-minute class, explain a sequence or make a suggestion such as 이 부분을 다시 해 볼까요? (Shall we try this part again?). Practice saying what you have learned, listening to the response, and explaining again.

After class · Optional co-creation — After-class co-creation is only for students who choose to join. Teams decide on a topic and format, then students choose roles in planning, scripting, performing, or editing. They can contribute through planning, writing, or editing without performing or being filmed. A dance-trained instructor guides students who choose choreography. Students listen to different views, ask why, explain their reasoning, and compare and revise ideas and wording suggested by AI. By explaining what they made together, they practise critical thinking, discussion, collaboration, and communication in Korean.
Movement before learning, gestures that express word meanings, and activities that involve everyone. Explore the sources behind each idea and how LAB plans to use them.

Harvard Medical School · Naperville · Expert commentary · School practice
Harvard Medical School’s John Ratey explains the relationship between exercise, memory, and concentration. Naperville Central High School ran LRPE, placing physical activity before reading and mathematics classes.
In a Harvard Health interview, John Ratey explains that regular exercise may affect brain regions involved in memory and the neurotrophic factor BDNF. Naperville’s LRPE is a school example focused on this connection between physical activity and learning. A 2013 Illinois Public Health Institute case report describes physical education scheduled before reading and mathematics classes for students who needed learning support.
How LAB designs its classes: This informs our plans for K-POP rhythm and movement before class. We choose activities students can enjoy, then adjust duration and intensity by observing fatigue and participation in the lesson afterward.

Schools on the Move · Finland’s national program
Finland promoted Schools on the Move nationally to add movement during lessons and breaks. School staff reported benefits for learning and the school atmosphere.
Schools on the Move is a program with strategic leadership from Finland’s Ministry of Education and Culture and National Agency for Education, and coordination by JAMK University of Applied Sciences. Rather than a single university experiment, it lets schools increase movement and student participation in ways suited to their circumstances. Official program information and its interim report describe reducing prolonged sitting and involving students in planning activities.
How LAB designs its classes: We connect movement before class with Korean lessons, while preparing after-class co-creation as an optional activity. Roles beyond dance include planning, scripting, and editing, so students can practise listening to and resolving different views.

Max Planck Institute · Vocabulary research in cognitive and brain science
In a 2015 study, participants who performed gestures matching the meanings of unfamiliar words they heard remembered the words better. Meaningful pictures also helped memory.
Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences had participants learn unfamiliar words from an artificial language in several ways. Performing gestures or viewing pictures that matched the meanings helped vocabulary memory compared with listening alone. Watching a movement and performing it produced different results; the connection between the word’s meaning and the movement matters.
How LAB designs its classes: We choose gestures and images that fit the meanings of the Korean being learned. Students use the expressions to describe the order of movements or explain them to classmates, then use them again in cultural projects after class.

These sources inform LAB’s class design. They do not indicate partnerships or accreditation from these institutions, or verified results for LAB’s K-POP classes. LAB’s program is in preparation, and learning outcomes will be assessed during actual operation.

Is after-class co-creation required? — No. Only students who want to join take part in the after-class co-creation program. They can choose planning, scripting, comparing meanings, or editing without dancing, performing, or being filmed. Students decide whether to participate and which role they want.

Has research directly compared exercise and language learning? — A 2007 study by Winter and colleagues compared new vocabulary learning among 27 healthy participants after intense running, low-intensity running, and rest. We refer to it as experimental evidence that exercise conditions can affect vocabulary learning. LAB does not use it as proof of K-POP class outcomes or to claim the same improvement rate for every learner.
You can explore LAB even if you have not decided to study abroad. You can start by exploring a subject that interests you, life in Korea, or something you would like to do in Korean.

On the LAB page you can watch short clips of real play from eight Korean games. Korean Racing, Words in Rhythm, Wind Run, Order Rush and Talk Rally practise listening; The Teacher Is Back, Entry Check and Blank Slice practise reading.

If you are new to Korean, racing’s picture-word stages or an easy song in Words in Rhythm are a good place to start, since they teach words through pictures and sound. Please enquire about course entry levels and availability, sharing your learning goal and current level.

This does not mean regular online classes are currently running. Share your learning goals and available times through the contact form or hello@synk.im to check preparation status and participation requirements.

Students’ education is not left entirely to AI. Check each program’s information for the actual teaching approach and teachers’ responsibilities.

We chose Level 4 with university classes and daily life in mind. Building on Level 3 Korean, learners practice reading more complex materials and explaining their opinions.
TOPIK II PBT · Out of 300 — Level 3: 120–149 points / Level 4: 150–189 points
TOPIK II IBT · Out of 600 — Level 3: 191–290 points / Level 4: 291–360 points
What we practice at LAB — Level 3: Describe familiar situations and give reasons and opinions / Level 4: Compare sources and opinions, and explain academic and social topics
University classes and graduation — Practice reading and writing for academic work. We also review the requirements of universities that ask for Level 4 or higher at graduation.
Scholarship requirements — Some universities offer different scholarships for Levels 3 and 4. We help learners prepare by checking the actual requirements of their chosen universities.

Part-time work requirements by year — TOPIK Level 4 is the Korean-language standard for part-time work in the third and fourth years of a bachelor’s degree. Language requirements, work permission, and individual circumstances must all be checked.

Part-time work · Language standards and permitted hours by year — The Korean-language standard for part-time work is TOPIK Level 3 for first- and second-year undergraduates, and Level 4 for third- and fourth-year undergraduates. For third- and fourth-year students, the guidance allows 10 weekday hours without the language requirement and 25 hours with it. Preferential conditions, such as university accreditation or grades, may allow 30 hours. Alternatives to TOPIK are also recognized. Before starting work, students need confirmation from their university and immigration permission for part-time employment.

Scholarships · How Level 3 and Level 4 benefits differ — Konyang University’s tuition scholarship guidance for new and transfer students lists 30% for TOPIK Level 3 and 50% for Level 4—a difference of 20 percentage points at the same university. These benefits do not apply to every university. Check the latest admissions guide for the relevant semester, admissions track, and scholarship renewal conditions.

Graduation · Language requirements after admission — The Korean proficiency needed for admission may differ from that required for graduation. For example, Sangmyung University lists TOPIK Level 4 or higher for Korean graduation certification in general academic fields. Requirements and accepted alternatives vary by university, department, and admission year. LAB chose Level 4 as a goal that looks beyond admission.

Work and visas · Language credentials and workplace preparation — TOPIK results can serve as evidence of Korean proficiency in employment and immigration reviews. Alongside Level 4 preparation, we plan practice in explaining experience at interviews and clarifying workplace tasks. Job-seeking status (D-10) and employment status (such as E-7) are different categories, with separate requirements for education, occupation, contracts, and more. Level 4 alone does not secure a work visa or resolve immigration matters.

Official guidance checked on September 18, 2026. The scores above are for TOPIK II; the speaking test is separate. The practice activities described are LAB’s curriculum design. A TOPIK level alone does not measure all speaking or workplace skills. Part-time work, scholarships, graduation, and immigration requirements vary by person and institution. Passing TOPIK is not guaranteed.

LAB develops textbooks, games, and a learning app together. We design them so students can use what they learn in practice and teachers can refer to that process to provide the help they need.
Textbooks and games — Practice grammar learned in Synapse Core through Synapse Talk conversations and scenario-based games. Tasks have clear purposes, such as making a request or sharing an opinion.

Eight textbooks — Connect understanding grammar with speaking and writing practice. Core covers material through Level 5 and Talk through Level 4.
Games and learning records — Use Korean in tasks with roles and goals, and compare your first draft with feedback.
Personalized learning app — We are developing one place to see tasks, hints, feedback, and learning records. When learning goals or preferred approaches change, the next lessons change with them.

Explain your study goals in a visa interview, ask for help at university, and describe your experience in a job interview. We are preparing VR learning that lets students practice situations they may face in real life.

Visa interview practice — We are preparing mock interviews within the one-year curriculum to help students organize their study goals and plans and answer questions. The aim is to explain their own plans clearly, rather than memorize answers.

Life in Korea and workplace experiences — Practice asking questions at university, clarifying work instructions, reporting problems, and requesting help. We also prepare job interview practice for explaining application reasons and experience.

How is a visa interview different from entry screening? — A visa interview may be requested by an overseas diplomatic mission during visa assessment. Entry screening is a separate process on arrival in Korea. LAB is preparing educational activities and mock practice to help learners explain their study goals and plans. This is not a visa application agency service or a guarantee of approval. Check the relevant diplomatic mission’s guidance for interview requirements and documents.
VR interview and workplace experiences are in preparation and are not yet formally offered. Activity records do not represent actual work experience or official qualifications.

Work toward TOPIK Level 4 while gaining experience for studying and living in Korea. Every 90-minute class includes a fixed 30 minutes of group speaking, connected with games, cultural activities, and personalized learning.

Korean for TOPIK Level 4 — Study grammar, listening, reading, and writing step by step, then use what you learn in conversations and scenario-based games. Practice both test formats and real communication.

Judgment and teamwork in the AI age — Choose a topic that reflects your interests and values, then develop a team project. Practice checking AI suggestions, listening to different views, finding agreement, and explaining your choices.

A portfolio for studying abroad — Organize your self-introduction, study plan, original and revised writing, presentation materials, and team roles. These materials help you prepare for classes and daily life in Korea and explain your experience.

Visa interviews and life in Korea — We are preparing mock interviews within the one-year program so learners can explain their study goals and plans in their own words. In VR, learners try interviews and unfamiliar daily situations first, then practice the difficult expressions again.

From the basics to Level 4: the learning stages — Build the foundations — Learn Hangul and basic sentence patterns, then speak and write in common situations such as introductions, ordering, and making plans. We also review each learner’s goals and current level.

Explain reasons and opinions — Add reasons to your ideas and check your understanding of others. Use what you learn in academic and everyday situations, such as making requests to professors and sharing ideas in team assignments.

Prepare for Level 4 and studying abroad — Practice listening, reading, and writing formats while comparing sources and organizing opinions. Presentations, interviews, and collaborative tasks connect test preparation with experience explaining ideas in practice.

Online learning support after the program — If you do not reach Level 4 on your first TOPIK test after the one-year program, we extend your academy app account free for six months to support online learning. Attendance or homework shortfalls do not disqualify you from this support. This is not an indefinite extension of in-person classes or a guarantee of passing.

Textbooks, games, and teachers work toward the same learning goals — The two Synapse Talk conversation books cover material through Level 4, and the six Synapse Core grammar books through Level 5. Level 4 is the main learning goal, not the limit of the textbooks. We are preparing a process in which students use textbook expressions in games, and teachers review their answers and revisions to plan further practice. Personalization separates what learners already know from what needs more practice, so their time goes where it is needed.

What conversation, English, and cultural activities include — Programs that include native Korean conversation and global English offer practice in introductions, questions, presentations, and understanding materials in both languages. K-POP and cultural activities provide opportunities to plan together and coordinate roles. The scope of conversation and English classes depends on the enrolled program. Schedules and conditions will be available in enrollment information.

Preparing for life and work in Korea — At LAB, learners study Korean, practice real situations, and organize learning and project work into a portfolio. Those who need more support with settling in Korea or finding work after graduation can ask about separate PATH services. PATH is preparing guidance and connections with schools and employers based on each learner’s intended major and career. LAB enrollment does not include every PATH service or guarantee admission or employment.

We are preparing to open and developing the curriculum, app, and VR program. TOPIK Level 4 is the program’s goal, not a guaranteed outcome. The portfolio documents work completed by the student; it does not replace official language scores or qualifications.
Learning to decide what to create and whom to create it for, rather than simply following AI output. We help learners use their values to guide choices, work with others, and review the results.

Values and philosophy · Find what guides your choices — Ask what kind of life you want and how you want to help others. When starting a project, choose its audience and purpose yourself. Practice respecting others’ choices while considering how your own ideas may affect them.

Creativity · Find ideas in your experience — Find topics in the culture you enjoy and difficulties you have experienced. Explore several approaches and make a small first draft. Compare AI suggestions, add your own experience and expression, and explain what you made different.

Cooperation and consideration · Understand each other’s roles — In crew activities, share roles such as planning, writing, performing, and editing. Ask what classmates find difficult and adjust participation and schedules together. Activities provide experience in doing your part and giving and receiving help.

Openness · Listen to other views and reconsider — When opinions differ, hear the other person’s reasons first. Decide which feedback to use and which choices to keep, with reasons. We encourage learners to try new approaches and revise their thinking when they find a stronger reason.

Judgment · Check AI suggestions and make a choice — Learn the basics of how AI works and its limits, and check its answers against source material. Compare your own draft with AI suggestions and choose what to use or revise. Also learn the responsibilities involved in handling personal information and other people’s creative work.

Expression · Explain your work and your reasons — Explain in Korean whom you created the work for, your role, and the choices you made. Listen and respond to questions after presenting. Organize both the finished work and revisions to show your interests and abilities through specific examples.

Why Korean and foundational learning still matter in the AI age — You need to read and understand sources to review AI answers, and express your own thinking to work with others. LAB connects discussion, writing, and cultural projects with Korean study for TOPIK Level 4. We design classes that distinguish trying independently, receiving necessary help, and explaining again without help, to see what students have actually learned.

Which sources inform this approach? · Checked September 18, 2026 — WEF’s 2025 employer survey highlights analytical and creative thinking, flexibility, self-awareness, and lifelong learning. UNESCO’s 2024 AI competency framework for students and the OECD–European Union’s 2026 AI literacy framework address human-centered judgment, creativity, collaboration, and responsible use. The OECD’s 2026 education outlook emphasizes that performing well on a task with AI is not the same as learning. LAB draws on these sources and its own educational philosophy to design the classes below. These sources do not demonstrate LAB’s educational outcomes or imply institutional accreditation.
Talk directly with native Korean teachers and use expressions learned in your textbooks. Refine your pronunciation and polite language, and practice answering unexpected questions in your own words.
English classes cover introductions and everyday conversation, then reading, emails, and presentations. We assess Korean and English separately to prepare classes suited to each learner’s level.

Native Korean conversation — Practice making requests, asking questions, and sharing opinions with a native Korean teacher. The teacher identifies points to improve in pronunciation, intonation, and polite language, and helps you express your meaning clearly. You use textbook grammar in conversation and learn which expressions fit the situation.

For example, you ask a professor for a meeting, learn that the time is unavailable, and suggest another time. When the teacher changes a question or condition, you adjust your response. After the conversation, review what was clear and what needs work, then try again. Practice the Korean needed to ask questions at university and request help in everyday life.

English classes — Start by introducing yourself and answering questions in English. Learners who need the basics listen to and say short sentences, then move on to reading in their field of interest, writing emails, presentations, and team activities. Lessons cover checking information and explaining opinions at school or work.

For example, write a message introducing a team project to an exchange student and answer questions about roles and schedules. With the teacher, add missing information and revise awkward expressions, then respond to a changed schedule or condition. The length of materials, difficulty of questions, and amount of explanation are adjusted to the learner’s English level and goals.

What if my Korean and English levels are different? — We assess Korean and English separately. If you are comfortable speaking Korean but new to English, for example, English classes begin with basic expressions. In each class, we review what learners say and write and prepare further practice for difficult pronunciation or expressions. Learners then try the same expressions in a different situation to check their understanding.

Which programs include these classes? — We are preparing a program focused on regular Korean classes and another that also includes native Korean conversation and English. Students who want conversation and English classes can choose a program that includes them. Check enrollment information or ask us about opening dates, teachers, class frequency, and what is included.

Native Korean conversation and English classes are in preparation. The situations above are sample class activities. Opening dates and what each program includes will be available in enrollment information.

LAB prepares learners for both language qualifications and real communication. We broaden practice situations so students can organize what they learn into test answers, talk with professors, and explain their experience in interviews. Our English teaching helps students read materials and work with others in ways that fit their intended major and career.

TOPIK · Put what you understand into speech and writing — Use vocabulary and grammar from Korean classes to answer a native teacher’s questions and explain your opinions. Write up the conversation afterward to compare spoken expressions with the written style used in test answers. Listening, reading, and writing are also practiced separately in the test formats.

Studying abroad · Ask questions, get help, and take part — Practice asking professors questions, agreeing on roles in team assignments, and checking information at university offices in Korean. English tasks include explaining opinions to international peers and reading short materials in your field or instructions for English-taught classes. Practice asking again and checking anything you did not understand.

Career preparation · Explain experience and clarify work — Describe your project role and the problems you solved in Korean, then answer follow-up interview questions. Students preparing for careers that require English also practice introductions, work emails, summaries, and short presentations. Beyond rehearsing answers, tasks include asking about unclear instructions and confirming schedules and results.

What will students take away? — Students build a portfolio of Korean request emails and opinion pieces they have written and revised, Korean and English introductions and project descriptions, expressions refined through teacher feedback, team roles, and presentation materials. Recording original wording alongside the reasons for revisions helps students explain their progress. Teachers use this work to suggest further practice, and students can revisit useful materials before a new semester or interview. The length and difficulty of the work depend on the student’s starting level and chosen program.

How are both languages used in one project? — For example, in a project creating a university guide for new international students, learners ask the university questions in Korean and organize the information they confirm. With an English teacher, they identify useful information in English guides and write a message for students from other countries. With a native Korean teacher, they explain the guide aloud and answer unexpected questions. Students compare AI translations or drafts with verified sources and explain why they chose the final wording.

Do English and native-speaker conversation help with TOPIK? — TOPIK II assesses Korean listening, reading, and writing; speaking is a separate test. We design listening, reading, and writing tasks that revisit vocabulary and expressions used in conversation to support test study. English is not assessed in TOPIK. LAB’s English classes help learners understand English materials and communicate in another language; we do not claim that the English classes themselves raise TOPIK scores.

How do you check language requirements for study and work? — Korean-taught and English-taught university programs may require different evidence of language proficiency. We first check the latest requirements of the chosen university and department, then distinguish preparation for official tests from practice needed to participate in classes. Career tasks are also based on the languages required by the intended role and job listing. Work completed in LAB classes does not replace official language scores or guarantee admission or employment.
Set your goals in Compass, then plan and create with others in crew projects. Teachers observe the work and conversations to provide feedback, and students record their revisions in a portfolio.

Set your goal with Compass — Talk about why you are learning Korean and what kind of life you want. Every eight-week season, choose a challenge and reflect on it. Your first answer is not fixed as the correct one. If your goal changes through experience, record why it changed.

Plan and finish a project with your crew — Use cultural activities to decide what your team wants to share and with whom. Divide the roles, create a draft, and review each other’s work along the way. Projects are designed so students make real decisions within their roles and see their work through to completion.

Use feedback and try again — Teachers review students’ questions, conversations about roles, and revisions. Together with students’ self-assessments, these help identify what support is needed next. Practice might begin with short explanations when presenting is difficult, or comparing sources when evidence is lacking.

Show your choices and growth in a portfolio — Alongside the finished work, organize your original goal, your own draft, your role, and the reasons for revisions. Prepare materials that let you explain, in your own words, what matters to you and what you have tried. Reflect on them when choosing a goal for the next season.

Sample cultural project · Introducing K-culture to a newcomer — Choose music, food, or a game as a team and ask what someone encountering it for the first time might want to know. Decide whether to use a performance, introduction video, or short guide, and write the Korean script yourselves. A team that values everyone’s participation, for example, can make roles for classmates who find dancing difficult. Coordinate schedules and roles, check AI wording suggestions, sources, and usage terms, then revise in response to each other’s reactions. In the presentation, explain why you chose the topic and format and what you changed. This sample activity connects the enjoyment of culture with choices that reflect consideration and values.

How do personalized learning and teachers work together? — We are developing a way to adjust support and the next task by considering the student’s stated goals, completed tasks, and teacher observations together. We do not judge personality from a single activity or score personal values. Automatically connecting classroom observations with all tasks, carrying learning records across devices, and collecting portfolio materials automatically remain development work.

What experience do you want students to leave with? — The experience of expressing an opinion, listening to others, and completing something together. In the next project, learners choose their roles and the support they need more precisely. For LAB, leadership means setting your own direction while collaborating responsibly with others. We support students in finding reasons for their choices, without choosing their interests or careers for them.

The program connecting Compass, crew projects, and portfolios is in preparation. The project above is an example of class design, not a record of actual student performance or measured skill improvement.
Form your own view, listen to classmates’ reasons, and coordinate what you will do together. In class, learners consider others while making and explaining their own final decisions.

Start with your own view — Each learner prepares an opinion on the same situation or task. Decide what you would choose and why, then share it with the group. This is practice in forming your own judgment before hearing other people’s answers.

Listen and find agreement — Take turns speaking and ask again when something is unclear. When opinions differ, listen to the reasons and discuss how everyone can participate. Practice expressing your ideas while considering others and working together.

Explain your decision and reasons — After the discussion, decide which parts of your original view to keep or change. Distinguish what the group agreed on from your own judgment, and explain your reasons. The teacher helps with expressions while guiding students to find and explain their own reasons.

How are the 30 minutes used? — This is group activity time within the 90-minute class. It is not an extra 30 minutes or 30 minutes of solo speaking per student. Learners practice speaking, listening, asking questions, and coordinating, while the teacher checks that the conversation is not dominated by a few students. Task difficulty and support are adjusted to the learners’ levels, while the group speaking time remains fixed.
These are operating guidelines for the regular classes currently in preparation. Cooperation, consideration, and judgment are skills we work on, not measured improvement results.

docs.title: SYNK SHIFT — AI and personalized services
paragraphs: SHIFT starts with one task where customers or staff need different guidance. We define who should complete what, then connect company materials and specialist modules with the shared Atlas engines. After introduction, we refine the service with the responsible team by checking actual use and the work needed to operate it.

SHIFT focuses on introducing and operating personalization for one client task. Training, consulting, automation, branding, research and testing are prepared where they support that introduction, use and validation. The direction is to expand into APIs and engine licensing after repeatable delivery and profitability have been checked.

Introduction and operation are in preparation. Features, system connections, operating responsibilities, support, timing and pricing are agreed for each actual engagement. Customer operations, effects and profitability have not yet been validated; the changes below are goals to check after introduction.

Start with one task.
Introduce personalization.

SYNK SHIFT is preparing to introduce and operate a personalized service for one company task. We connect company materials and rules with the shared Atlas engines and the specialist modules needed to provide guidance for customer and staff conditions. The use cases below are candidates; scope, operating responsibilities, timing and pricing are agreed for each actual engagement.

We prepare introduction and operation for companies and institutions whose customers or staff need personalized guidance. We begin with one task for which materials are available and results can be checked. Purchasing advice, software usage guidance, expert coaching and sales or customer-service training are candidate use cases. Before company size, we check the materials available, the task to validate and operating responsibilities.

We first define the users and completion criteria for one task, the materials and system connections, and operating responsibilities. We prepare the agreed personalized service, instructions for the team to use and operate it, checks, exception handling and follow-up support scope.

Training, consulting, automation, branding, research and testing support this introduction and use. Actual features, deliverables, editable source scope, timing and pricing are agreed in each introduction contract. Live client operation, effects and profitability have not yet been validated.
We show how SYNK uses AI to make actual work and content. We explain the problem, the request made to AI and why a person changed the result, based on actual work.

SHIFT’s new business focuses on introducing and operating personalization for one client task. AI education and work support are prepared where they help that introduction, and experimental features are not presented as client results.
The finished result alone does not explain how it was made. SHIFT shares the approaches tried, what failed, and the reasons behind revisions and decisions so you can draw on them in your own work.

For example, adding decorative stitching to both the SYNK wordmark and the business names made the website logos difficult to read. We kept the soft texture but reduced the stitching on SYNK so the colors and details of LAB, SHIFT, and PULSE could stand out.
We wanted to make the characters and objects from our screens in the real world, too. We designed their soft textures with objects you could touch and keep nearby in mind.
We built the Loom engine to bring those textures to the screen and make them feel alive through small movements and responses.
In this example, we decided which text should be read first, then adjusted the other decoration. This is an actual design revision, not evidence of a measured effect on customer response or sales.

We prepare the training, consulting, workflow automation and branding needed to introduce and use a personalized service. Support covers how staff use it, how it connects with existing work, and the explanations and screens customers see.
Training and consulting — Staff learn to use the service with real work materials, check its results and handle exceptions. We also agree on the scope and operating approach for the task.
Workflow automation and system connections — We define which steps the service handles and which need a person, then connect the recurring tasks and existing systems needed.
Branding and usage guidance — We shape the service’s explanations, screens and guidance to fit your brand and help customers understand who it is for and how it helps.
We agree on the support scope, deliverables, staff training and follow-up support for the task being introduced.

We are preparing personalized services in two areas: purchasing and product use, and coaching and training. They help customers choose and use products, or adapt expert coaching and staff training to each person. We agree together on the task and features to introduce.

Personalized buying and quote advice — When a customer enters their budget, intended use, and the equipment they already have, it first shows a fitting set, the reasons for it, and the options they can leave out.
A good fit for: sellers and specialist shops with many products and options, where every consultation starts by asking about budget and use again
What you get: A web consultation service that answers with your products, and a summary of each customer’s requirements for your staff.
What changes: Customers enquire after seeing the products that fit them and why. Your staff receive organized requirements and start with the quote.

Product onboarding and adoption support — It looks at the customer’s role, goal, and how far they have got, and guides them through what to do now, one step at a time.
A good fit for: software and B2B service companies whose new customers stall at setup or keep asking the same usage questions
What you get: A web guide your customers follow by themselves.
What changes: Customers see the next step right away instead of waiting for a reply. Your support team spends its time on problems that need a person.

Expert coaching service development — It carries the expert’s method and criteria, giving each client different tasks and feedback. It changes the next task after seeing the results.
A good fit for: instructors, consultants, and training companies who repeat the same tasks and explanations one by one as clients grow
What you get: A coaching service for clients, with diagnosis, individual tasks, and follow-up guidance in one flow.
What changes: The service takes over the repeated guidance. The expert spends time on the judgement and advanced coaching that need them in person.

Sales and customer service practice — Staff practise realistic situations with your products and service standards. What they miss comes back in the next practice.
A good fit for: sales and customer-service teams and franchise head offices whose staff were trained but cannot put it into words in front of a real customer
What you get: A training tool for staff, with situation practice and follow-up tasks.
What changes: Staff try difficult replies many times before the real thing. Managers see what each person missed and coach from there.

Atlas is the name of eight shared engines developed by SYNK. We combine them with modules for product information and specialist criteria, rather than rebuilding the shared engines for each company. SHIFT connects client materials, rules and systems, and defines completion criteria and operating methods for the chosen task.
It asks only what it needs — It starts with the requirements that change the choice, and is built not to ask again what was already answered.
It recommends with reasons — It shows why something is recommended or left out, so customers can judge whether it fits them.
It adjusts after seeing the result — It sees where someone got stuck and changes the next guidance and practice, because each person falls short in different places.
User conditions and activity records are used within the purposes and consent agreed for the actual introduction. Local engine validation is not presented as evidence of client results.

We prepare introduction training using examples close to actual work so team members new to AI can use the personalized service. They practice writing specific requests, checking results and correcting the parts that need it.
The training and practice needed for the personalization introduction are scoped and scheduled for the team’s experience and tasks.

The character-making guide is no longer offered. The SHIFT page now presents four possible applications of personalized services, along with training, consulting, workflow automation, and branding support for adopting and using them.
If you are looking for materials or training for your work, tell us who will use them, what you want to solve, and what results you need. We will confirm what we can do and the schedule.

We prepare the AI training and practice needed by the team introducing and operating the personalized service. They practice making requests with actual work materials, comparing and correcting results, and handling exceptions.

Training is scoped as support for that introduction, not a separate new core product line. Participants, responsible people, timing and costs are checked for each actual engagement. This does not mean institutional agreements or accredited courses are operating.

We do not guarantee the same results as the public examples. Results may vary with the working environment, tools, and requests. Our own production examples cannot establish a promise of business success, revenue, or time savings.
After introduction, we compare completion, errors, time and introduction and support costs with the existing method. Live client operations, effects and profitability have not yet been validated.
Where work can be shared publicly, we also show failures and revisions. Using actual work, we explain what we asked for, what came back, and why we changed the approach.
We do not publish private student or client materials or internal operating documents.
Start with one task. Put personalization to work.

Introduction and operation are in preparation. Features, system connections, operating responsibilities, support, timing and pricing are agreed for each actual engagement. Customer operations, effects and profitability have not yet been validated; the changes below are goals to check after introduction. API and engine licensing are later expansion directions, not products currently for sale.
We begin with the users and the result they should complete. We connect company materials and rules, check the service in its actual environment, and agree who will operate it and handle exceptions.
Task and completion criteria — We define who should complete what and the existing method. We also agree the materials, personal data scope and exceptions that need a person’s review.

Connections, introduction and team preparation — We combine shared engines with the specialist modules needed to connect client materials and systems. We check the actual use environment and prepare the team to operate the service.
Check use and operation — We examine completion, errors, time and support workload together. We document what can be changed, responsibilities for checks, exceptions and support, and follow-up work.
This is currently in preparation. Use cases and an enquiry channel do not establish a launched service, contract availability, pricing or live client operations.

We research the customers and environments for a personalized service, then use hands-on product tests to identify improvements. We check who needs what and whether the service helps more than the existing approach.
User and market research — We define the users and task, and examine their conditions and difficulties with the existing method through interviews and materials.
Usability testing — We watch where participants stop and what explanation they need while they use it themselves.

Check results and operating work — We check completion, errors, time and the work required for introduction and support together. We distinguish observations from interpretation and choose the next improvement.

This introduction validation support is in preparation. Audience, participation, consent, compensation, timing and costs are agreed within the introduction scope. A small set of responses is not generalized to the whole market, and results are not guaranteed.

SHIFT is preparing to introduce and operate personalized services for one client task by combining SYNK’s eight shared Atlas engines with the specialist modules needed. Company product materials, manuals and expert criteria connect with user conditions and activity results to change the questions, recommendation reasons and next guidance.

We combine shared personalization capabilities with task-specific expertise instead of rebuilding Atlas for each company. SHIFT defines scope, materials, completion criteria and team operation. We first check actual effects and support costs, validate repeatable delivery, then consider API and engine licensing products. Launch, pricing, client effects and profitability have not yet been established or validated.
We first check usefulness in one client’s actual task, along with delivery and support costs. API and engine licensing products are considered after a repeatable delivery scope has been validated.
Introduce and operate one task — Define the users, completion result, materials and operating responsibilities for one task.
Validate repeatable delivery — Check the common scope that can be delivered to other clients, introduction and support costs, and profitability.
API and engine licensing — Consider productizing capabilities with validated repeatable delivery and operation. Launch timing, pricing and terms have not yet been set.
API and engine licensing are later expansion directions, not products currently for sale.
Initial setup and ongoing use and operation are scoped separately in the agreement. We also agree in advance on the scope and cost of additional usage or new features.
Initial setup fee — We organize the task and materials, configure the service and connect it with existing systems. Deliverables and acceptance criteria are agreed together.
Recurring service and operation fee — This covers service use, quality checks and agreed operational support. We define usage allowances, material updates, support hours and error handling.

Additional usage and development fees — We confirm the scope and cost in advance for usage beyond the allowance, new system connections or feature changes. Agreed error fixes remain within the existing responsibilities.
Pricing, allowances and contract terms have not yet been set and will be discussed for each task and operating scope.

docs.title: SYNK PULSE — Films, content and IP
paragraphs: For a film a brand commissions, we first decide where it will be used and who will see it. PULSE’s own music, videos, and character stories aim to be work you want to hear and see again. Both use two of Atlas’s engines in production: Loom, which composes the screen, and Reed, which handles sound.
We also welcome inquiries about creative collaborations, licensing, and advertising.

We create ad videos, model images and lookbooks, alongside online content, original IP, licensing, co-production and advertising collaborations. We distinguish released work from services in preparation. We do not collect personal viewing responses into learning or emotional profiles or promise educational or therapeutic effects. AI portraits, introduction decks, and studio and equipment rental are in preparation, with bookings not yet open. Locations, available equipment, dates, prices and on-site support will be announced once decided.

From ad and model videos
to music and characters

SYNK PULSE creates product ads, brand films, AI model images, lookbooks and how-to videos, alongside music, character content and IP. We are also preparing AI portraits made from existing photos, introduction decks, and studio and equipment rental.

We create music for reading, working, and resting, along with videos that bring music and scenes together. We check that the sound and visuals complement each other and flow naturally from beginning to end.

“The Brightest Person Tonight” is a full-song video lasting 1 minute and 1.6 seconds. It includes music and scenes from a Chuseok courtyard, notes about the song and scenes, and production credits. The K-LOFI 24 live radio stream is listed separately on YouTube.
PULSE's music, videos, characters, and stories are created to be enjoyed. Not all of them are designed for Korean learning. LAB prepares Korean education and learning content.
We value enjoyment and the feeling a work evokes, but we do not guarantee that listening or viewing alone improves Korean skills or concentration, or provides therapeutic benefits.
We are preparing our service so that personal listening activity is not collected to build educational, emotional, or concentration profiles.

You can ask about music, video, character, and story production collaborations, licensing, advertising, and ad and model video production. Tell us what work you need, where you will use it, your audience, preferred schedule, and required file formats. For ad and model videos, the PULSE video brief helps you set the direction first.
Production availability and usage terms are confirmed individually. The contract sets out production, ownership and usage rights, delivery files, revisions, and support.
Public examples do not confirm acceptance of a project or a delivery schedule. Advertising work owned by a client is not treated as SYNK-owned creative work.

A public listening or viewing link does not grant permission to redistribute a work, put it in a video, play it in a shop, or use it in advertising or commercially. Please confirm availability and rights first.
To start an inquiry, email hello@synk.im with the work title, media, location, duration, and intended use. This question panel does not grant permission or make a final copyright determination.
K-LOFI 24 is music content from SYNK PULSE. We create music and videos to enjoy while working or resting.

The K-LOFI page has YouTube listening links and information about planned music releases. Check YouTube for the current broadcast status. The full-song video for “The Brightest Person Tonight” is available separately from the live stream.
Films for brands fit their purpose; our own work invites a second look.
We create online content to enjoy in everyday life, carefully shaping the sound, visuals, and flow of each story.
Music and video — We make music and videos for reading, working, or taking a break. Find our public channels on the SYNK Radio listening page.

Characters and stories — Our stories grow from the personalities and relationships of Mongle, Kkamong, and Marin. We shape their actions and scenes for each format, from short videos to continuing stories.
We develop original IP through our characters, music, and stories. We collaborate on licensing and co-production with agreed terms.
Characters and their world — We maintain the characters' appearance, personalities, relationships, and stories together, keeping them recognizable across new work.

Using and licensing our work — We review the intended use, media, and duration for music, video, or characters and agree on the scope. Public availability for listening or viewing does not mean permission for commercial use.
Co-production — We plan a work together around the purpose of the collaboration. We agree on the production scope, rights, and release plan, then develop it in a way that suits the work.
We make brand advertising with PULSE music and characters. We explore how music, video, and characters can work with your message and release channels.
Agree on the plan and usage terms — We first clarify the advertising goal, production scope, rights, and usage terms. We also agree on any required advertising disclosures.
Personalized service adoption with SHIFT — SHIFT handles usage guidance and design updates for personalized services. PULSE focuses on creative production and advertising collaborations.
We distinguish published work from services in preparation. Contact us to confirm the scope and schedule for production, licensing, or advertising collaborations.

We make product ads, brand films, AI model images and lookbooks, and how-to videos, from planning to the finished piece. You receive them in formats ready for your website, product pages, and social media.
Together we choose between AI video and live shooting, whichever suits the brand.

Product ads — We turn the product’s details and real use into a short ad, and make edits for each channel from the same source.
A good fit for: brands whose product has clear strengths that photos and long text fail to convey
What you get: A product ad, edits for social media, and images for product pages and ads.
What changes: Customers see the features and the product in use, and decide whether to buy. You do not need to commission each channel separately.

Brand films & commercials — We put what your company does and does well into one film, with edits for your website, sales, and events.
A good fit for: companies whose introduction changes with whoever gives it
What you get: A brand film and edits for your website, sales, and events.
What changes: Anyone can show a new customer the same introduction. The same film works in proposals, on your website, and at events.

AI models & lookbooks — We make product images, lookbooks, and fashion films with the AI model the brand chooses. Colour and fit are checked against reference photos.
A good fit for: brands that keep needing worn shots and in-use scenes for product pages and social media
What you get: Product images worn or used by an AI model, a lookbook, and a fashion film.
What changes: One model and mood keep the whole range consistent. When a new product arrives, you can continue with the same model.

docs.title: SYNK — Our philosophy
paragraphs: SYNK builds a personalization engine. We started with Korean education. In classrooms in Ulaanbaatar, we saw that every student had different strengths, got stuck in different places, and had different reasons for learning, so we set out to use technology to teach each student in a way that fits them. The engine we built is Atlas.
Five principles guide how SYNK works.

We build all eight engines ourselves — Eight engines share the work, from deciding what is needed to ordering what to learn, recording what you tried, giving explanations and hints, and checking whether the help worked. The same team makes the felt screens, the music, and the sound, so what we tailor to one person can also reach them through what they see and hear.

We don’t guess from age — We adapt to the settings you choose and the results of what you actually tried, not to your age, gender, or nationality. When your goal changes, the next practice and suggestion change with it, and we tell you why we prepared them.

We check whether the help worked — Finishing something is not proof that you improved. We look separately at whether what you did without help got better, whether the suggestions were right, and whether it was comfortable to use. We do not roll out a new method if results get worse for any group, whether people in their 20s or their 60s.

We keep your answers apart from AI’s guesses — Your own answers, what you actually did, and what a teacher observed are kept as originals. Anything AI corrected or inferred is marked separately, so you can check it and correct it.

Built for anyone, built to last — You choose larger text, shorter explanations, and ways to use it without sound, and we refine each step so a first-time user knows what to do next. Free features calculate on your device without going through an AI server, so the service can keep running as more people use it.
We build the engine, services, and content to these standards. We tell you what is still in development and what you can use now; see each brand page for what is available.
We check whether explanations are clear, interfaces are easy to use, and the promised features work properly.
We use AI to help with repetitive recording, organization, and production. People understand one another, build relationships, and make important decisions.

When students change their goals or preferences, their education should be able to reflect that. We record what students say, what teachers observe, and what AI infers as distinct types of information.
We distinguish between what is planned, what has been built, what is actually in use, and what has demonstrated results.

records.answer:
SYNK LAB is preparing 10 minigames. On the LAB page you can watch real gameplay from eight Korean games: Korean Racing, Words in Rhythm, Wind Run, Order Rush and Talk Rally practise listening, while The Teacher Is Back, Entry Check and Blank Slice practise reading. All eight are prototypes.

Race along a coastal road with Marin or Kkamong, listen to a Korean question, and answer by driving into a picture or word lane. Correct answers trigger a boost. The prototype includes 2,000 basic and extended vocabulary items, 400 learning stages of five words, and 2,008 word and guidance voice clips. All stages share one coastal course; the vocabulary list does not guarantee coverage of every TOPIK Level 1–2 item. Use A/D or arrow keys, or mobile steering and answer buttons.

Narration sequences each question, word pronunciation, and correct/incorrect feedback. Engine volume falls while speech plays, and the car waits before the gate until the question finishes. Replay, optional listening captions, pronunciation after the race, and a review that prioritizes mistakes support practice. The commentary is scripted audio, rather than live AI conversation.

Listening connects word sounds with pictures and spelling; reading practises recognizing spelling and meaning. Words in Rhythm plays three of our own Korean songs across two lanes. Listen to a narrated sentence and question, then answer O/X. Music quietens and regular notes clear during narration. Practise understanding times, places, reasons, conditions and changed information, with timing and listening answers checked separately and new spoken review questions. Speaking and writing extend expressions into offline dialogue and sentence tasks. The games currently provide no pronunciation or free-writing assessment. TOPIK I tests listening and reading; TOPIK II includes writing, while TOPIK Speaking is a separate test.

In Wind Run you hear 16 short requests such as “Take the left path.” or “Jump over the low fence.” and act them out. While you run there is only sound, no text; the text appears in the practice before the run and the review after it. In Order Rush you hear café orders and make each drink, matching the number of cups, the temperature and what to leave out. In Talk Rally, Mongle says something in Korean as it hits the ball, and you hit it back toward the reply card that fits. In The Teacher Is Back you read the requests in a story and move Marin and Kkamong to tidy the classroom, then read new, changed requests at the end. In Entry Check you read a notice, check each guest’s ticket, bags and words, and stamp pass or reject. In Blank Slice you read a sentence with a blank and slash the one word piece out of four that fits.

A meta-analysis of digital game-based second-language learning reported a between-group effect size of d=0.50 (Dixon et al., 2022). A retrieval-practice meta-analysis covering 222 studies and 48,478 learners reported g=0.499 (Yang et al., 2021). Picture-and-audio effects vary with materials and pacing (Reinwein, 2012). These findings inform our recall, feedback, short-audio, and replay design. Effect sizes are not percentage improvements, and SYNK-specific TOPIK gains and long-term learning outcomes have not yet been tested with learners. Primary sources are linked in the learning showcase.

We are preparing a path from minigames and offline learning toward TOPIK Level 1, followed by everyday-life content and village NPC conversations. The planned unlock follows an in-app TOPIK Level 1+ foundation stage and does not require an official score report. The full ten-game set, classroom-to-village integration, and NPC connection are still in preparation. The games store anonymous progress in this browser only, racing’s automated demonstrations are left out of learning records, and nothing connects to student accounts or a server.
